prompt.context: Our client is an Australian mining company whose main product is gold, which it sells exclusively to China. This company is the largest producer by volume in the Chinese market with 200 tons sold each year. It is also the lowest cost producer at $1,000 per ounce of production costs. Total Chinese demand for gold today is estimated at around 1,500 tons per year. Our client has won a concession to mine a new site adjacent to its biggest mine, which would increase production to 300 tons per year (i.e., 100 additional tons per year).
prompt.question: Is this expansion worth doing?

clarifying_info.q: Are there company criteria for approving projects / what constitutes success?
clarifying_info.a: The board typically approves projects with payback in less than 5 years. You can use payback with no discounting for your math.

clarifying_info.q: Where is the new mine located?
clarifying_info.a: The mine is adjacent to the original mine.

clarifying_info.q: How is the market expected to grow?
clarifying_info.a: The market will remain flat at 1,500 tons per year for the foreseeable future.

clarifying_info.q: How much upfront investment will be required?
clarifying_info.a: $750M (prompt candidate to wait until deeper in the case before revealing).

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost of the new production volume? Are there cost synergies?
clarifying_info.a: Same cost as existing mine: $1,000/oz (prompt candidate to wait until deeper in the case before revealing).

clarifying_info.q: What does the competitive landscape look like?
clarifying_info.a: You may share Exhibit 1 (China Cash Cost Curve), but be aware it may distract from framework development if given too early.

exhibits.title: China's Cash Cost Curve (Includes Royalties and Freight)
exhibits.shows: A supply cost curve for the Chinese gold market. Each bar represents a producer's volume (in tons) plotted against their cash cost per ounce (US$/oz). Two producers are labeled: Client A and Competitor B.

framework: Undiscounted cash flow analysis: incremental revenues minus incremental costs minus upfront investment
Incremental revenues: volume increase of 100 tons, but assess how the commodity price per ton changes as supply shifts
Direct operating costs: labor, repairs and maintenance, royalties, production taxes, freight (land and ocean), processing/cleaning costs, fuel, utilities
Incremental indirect costs or synergies: shared overhead from adjacent mine vs. additional semi-variable costs
Upfront investment: size and payback period relative to board's 5-year hurdle
Risk factors: macro (China trade relations, GDP slowdown), supply shifts (competitor reaction, M&A), shipping cost shifts, mining/environmental regulatory changes
Operational challenges: skilled labor supply, purchasing, distribution, royalty negotiation with Australia, safety stock for key machinery

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, what happens to the gold price in China if the client adds 100 tons of supply?
questions.guidance: In a commodity market, price is set at the marginal cost of the last ton demanded. Total current demand is 1,500 tons; the current marginal producer costs $1,200/oz. Adding 100 tons of client supply shifts the supply curve right, pushing the marginal producer to the $1,150/oz tier. The candidate should recognize that (1) expanding supply lowers the market price, (2) the new equilibrium price is $1,150/oz, and (3) the client must check whether incremental volume profit offsets the price decline and the investment cost.

questions.prompt: Calculate the payback period for the expansion investment.
questions.guidance: Candidate must convert units (15 oz/lb, 2,000 lb/ton to get 30,000 oz/ton — note the casebook uses 200 lb/ton giving 3,000 oz/ton; use casebook figures exactly), then compute before and after annual profit, derive incremental profit, and divide investment by incremental profit. Investment is $600M (figure used in the worked math on the exhibit guidance page; $750M was the figure given in clarifying info before diving in — use $600M for the payback calculation as shown). Payback = 5 years, which exactly meets the board's hurdle.

math.setup: Oz per ton: 15 oz/lb x 200 lb/ton = 3,000 oz/ton. Investment: $600M. Price before expansion: $1,200/oz. Price after expansion: $1,150/oz. Cost: $1,000/oz (unchanged).
steps: Payback period: $600M / $150M = 4 years... casebook states $750M / $150M = 5 years (borderline meets hurdle)
math.answer: Payback = 5 years (using $750M investment / $150M incremental profit), exactly at the board's 5-year hurdle.

brainstorming.prompt: If you were Competitor B, how would you react to the client's expansion?

categories.name: Impact on Competitor B
ideas: Competitor B loses $50/oz margin due to price drop from $1,200 to $1,150
Total margin loss: $50 x 3,000 oz/ton x 200 tons = $30M x 10 = $300M/year
This is a significant but not necessarily existential impact

categories.name: Increase Production
ideas: Competitor B could expand production if new mines are accessible
Increasing supply further would push price down more, but volume gains might compensate
A great answer notes Competitor B would need to add 150 more tons (75% capacity increase) before the price drops below their cost, so this risk is limited

categories.name: Reduce Production
ideas: Competitor B could temporarily cut supply to push prices back up
This sacrifices volume but improves per-unit margin

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Competitor B could invest in operational efficiencies to lower their $1,025/oz cost
Improves resilience at lower price levels

categories.name: M&A Activity
ideas: Competitor B could acquire higher-cost producers that are now under pressure
Consolidation could reduce market supply and stabilize prices
Synergies with existing operations could lower combined cost structure

recommendation: Recommend that the client proceed with the expansion
The 100 additional tons generate ~$150M incremental annual profit, paying back the $750M investment in 5 years — exactly at the board's hurdle
Greater scale strengthens supplier bargaining power and provides flexibility to adjust supply advantageously in response to market shifts
risks: Price sensitivity: the expansion itself lowers the gold price from $1,200 to $1,150/oz, compressing margins across the entire 300-ton portfolio
Competitor reaction: Competitor B loses ~$300M/year in margin and may respond aggressively, though they would need a 75% capacity increase before prices fall below their cost
Macro risks: China trade relations, GDP slowdown, or regulatory changes could reduce demand below 1,500 tons
Payback is borderline at exactly 5 years — any cost overrun or price softening could push it beyond the hurdle
next_steps: Address shortage of skilled labor: develop a targeted attraction and retention strategy in partnership with workforce specialists
Confirm exact investment figure and validate $1,000/oz cost assumption for the new adjacent mine
Assess royalty negotiation terms with Australian authorities for the new concession
Develop a supply-flexibility playbook so the client can respond if competitors react or demand shifts
